---
title: "Working on Longleaf"
description: "Essential shell commands and software modules for working on Longleaf."
---

## Essential shell commands

After logging in, you work at a **shell prompt**. These commands are enough to navigate Longleaf, organize files, and prepare a job:

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Show the current directory | `pwd` |
| List files | `ls` |
| Enter a directory | `cd directory-name` |
| Move up one directory | `cd ..` |
| Go to your home directory | `cd ~` |
| Create a directory | `mkdir directory-name` |
| Print a short file | `cat filename` |
| Edit a text file | `nano filename` |
| Leave Longleaf | `exit` |

`~` is shorthand for your home directory, so `cd ~/example2_single_job` works from anywhere. Commands and filenames are case-sensitive: `Results` and `results` are different names.

`nano` is a small editor that runs in the terminal. Press Ctrl+O and Enter to save, then Ctrl+X to exit. FileZilla's View/Edit feature, introduced in Module 2, is an alternative for people who prefer editing on their own computer.

## Software modules

Basic Linux tools are available when you log in. Longleaf uses **software modules** to provide additional programs and to let different versions of the same program coexist.

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| See available software | `module avail` |
| Search for R modules | `module avail r` |
| Load the default R module | `module add r` |
| Load a particular version | `module add r/<version>` |
| Show loaded modules | `module list` |
| Unload all modules | `module purge` |

For example, `module add r` makes the default R installation available in the current session. Use `module avail r` first if a project requires a particular version.

### Put module commands in job scripts

By default, `sbatch` carries much of the environment from the submitting shell into a job. A reproducible script should not depend on whatever happened to be loaded at submission time. UNC recommends explicitly resetting the modules and then loading what the job needs:

```bash
module purge
module add r
```

`module save` can arrange for a preferred set of modules to load at future logins, but batch jobs should still contain their own `module purge` and `module add` commands.

### Pin versions when reproducibility requires it

The default version of a program can change. A short exploratory task may be fine with `module add r`; a project that must be rerun months later should record and load the version it used. Replace `<version>` with one shown by `module avail r`:

```bash
module purge
module add r/<version>
```
